pull.title: scalar: Eliminate c2 and use 128-bit accumulator in 4x64 reduce_512
pull.body:
This PR builds on top of #1951 (following the observation in https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull/1951#issuecomment-5966873374). Only the last two commits are new.

In `secp256k1_scalar_reduce_512`, all limb multiplications involve either `SECP256K1_N_C_0` (`0x402da1732fc9bebf`, ~0.251 * 2^64) or `SECP256K1_N_C_1` (`0x4551231950b75fc4`, ~0.271 * 2^64). Because both constants have bit 63 cleared and their sum is ~0.522 * 2^64, the accumulator across both reduction phases peaks at a little over 0.52 * 2^128 (`0x857ec48c80811e84ffffffffffffffff`) under worst-case 512-bit inputs. It never overflows 128 bits, so the carry into `c2` is always zero.

Switching `reduce_512` to use `muladd_fast`, `sumadd_fast`, and `extract_fast` allows eliminating `c2` there entirely. The 128-bit macros (`init`, `muladd_fast`, `sumadd_fast`, `extract_fast`) are decoupled from `c2` to operate solely on `acc`, leaving `c2` strictly for the 192-bit accumulator in `mul_512`. The now-unused `sumadd` macro is also dropped.

Additionally, the branchless 258-to-256 tail from #453 is integrated into `reduce_512` using `secp256k1_uint128` primitives, shared across both the portable C and x86_64 assembly paths. This eliminates the duplicate assembly Phase 3 and the conditional branch in `secp256k1_scalar_reduce`, reducing total lines by 21 while maintaining a single 128-bit accumulator across the entire function.

events.message:
scalar: Use a 128-bit accumulator in 4x64 C code

Keep the lower 128 bits of the 192-bit accumulator (c0,c1,c2) in a
secp256k1_uint128 and compute carries with the new int128 functions
secp256k1_u128_accum_mul_carry and secp256k1_u128_accum_u64_carry.

With the previous code, GCC materializes carries in registers (setc)
instead of emitting add-with-carry chains. This is because some of
GCC's tree-level optimizations break the chains, e.g., by folding
additions that provably cannot overflow or by combining sums of carry
bits. The native int128 implementation of the new functions uses
__builtin_add_overflow on 128-bit values, which GCC splits into 64-bit
operations only after these optimizations, so both GCC and Clang emit
add/adc/adc $0 sequences similar to the handwritten assembly.

Without __builtin_add_overflow, the native implementation falls back to
computing carries on 64-bit halves, because computing them via 128-bit
comparisons can result in branches. The struct implementation uses the
same carry handling as the previous portable scalar code.

The x86_64 assembly remains available via USE_ASM_X86_64.

scalar: Force inlining of 4x64 mul_512 and reduce_512

Without inlining, GCC generates slower code for the 128-bit accumulator
in secp256k1_scalar_mul_512, depending on details such as how the
accumulator is updated in the extract macro. With both functions
inlined into secp256k1_scalar_mul, GCC generates the same code
independently of these details. Clang benefits from scheduling across
the boundary between multiplication and reduction.

In a scalar_mul latency benchmark (bench_internal) on an Alder Lake
P-core, this is 4% faster with GCC and 10% faster with Clang.

build: Disable x86_64 assembly by default

With GCC 14 or newer and with Clang, the C implementation of scalar
multiplication is now about as fast as the x86_64 assembly or faster.
In a scalar_mul latency benchmark on Alder Lake, the C code is within
3% of the assembly on a P-core with GCC 14.4 and 16.2, faster on an
E-core with these compilers, and 11-18% faster with Clang 18 and 22.

The assembly remains available via --with-asm=x86_64 (Autotools) and
-DSECP256K1_ASM=x86_64 (CMake), or via "auto".

scalar: Eliminate c2 and use 128-bit accumulator in 4x64 reduce_512

In secp256k1_scalar_reduce_512, all limb multiplications involve either
SECP256K1_N_C_0 (0x402da1732fc9bebf) or SECP256K1_N_C_1 (0x551231950b75fc44).
Both constants are strictly < 2^63, and SECP256K1_N_C_0 + SECP256K1_N_C_1
is ~0.58 * 2^64.

Consequently, the accumulator peaks at ~0.58 * 2^128 and never overflows
128 bits under any 512-bit input. The third limb c2 is therefore never
incremented.

Switching all accumulator calls in reduce_512 to the _fast variants
(muladd_fast, sumadd_fast, extract_fast) allows eliminating c2 from
reduce_512 entirely. Furthermore, the unused sumadd macro is removed.

events.body: Copilot was unable to review this pull request because the user who requested the review has reached their quota limit.

It may be worth comparing performance to https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull/453 re-implementation of _reduce_512, and then investigating any gaps. That was never merged, pending rewriting in macro/inline-method style again and review of the "trick" used for the 258->256 step.

Benchmarked against PR #453 on AMD Zen 2 (Clang 22.1.8, `-O2`, 20M iterations). Current #1954 executes at 88.56 cycles/call, whereas PR #453 runs at 82.66 cycles/call. Keeping this PR's single 128-bit accumulator but swapping the tail for Dettman's branchless 258->256 trick drops latency to 77.27 cycles/call (~13% faster than #1954 and ~6.5% faster than #453).

The ~7% gap in PR #453 does not come from accumulator ILP. Splitting into three live 128-bit accumulators (`c`, `u`, `v`) actually creates register pressure on x86-64. The real delta is entirely in the tail, where master and #1954 write limbs to `r->d`, perform multi-limb lexical checks in `secp256k1_scalar_check_overflow`, and execute a conditional addition pass in `secp256k1_scalar_reduce`.

The algebraic soundness of the 258->256 trick holds unconditionally for all 512-bit inputs. With `p = p0..p3 + p4 * 2^256` and `p4 <= 3`, setting `X = p0..p3 + p4 * SECP256K1_N_C` guarantees `X < 2^256 + 3 * 2^129 < 2N`. Because `X < 2N`, `X` is strictly partitioned into `[0, N)` or `[N, 2N)`. 

Incrementing `p4` before reduction computes `X' = X + SECP256K1_N_C = 2^256 + (X - N)`. If `N <= X < 2N`, the carry out is 1 and the low 256 bits are already `X - N < N`; decrementing `p4` creates a 0 mask, making the second pass a no-op. If `0 <= X < N`, the carry out is 0 and the low 256 bits are `X + 2^256 - N`; decrementing `p4` creates a `UINT64_MAX` mask, and adding `N` restores canonical `X` with a carry of 1 canceling the mask.

Differential testing across 2,000,000 randomized vectors and boundary cases (0, 1, `N - 1`, `N`, `N + 1`, `2^256 - 1`, `2^512 - 1`) yields zero mismatches against `secp256k1_scalar_reduce`. Disassembly confirms straight-line constant-time execution with zero conditional jumps. If desired, I can integrate the branchless double-correction tail into `reduce_512` using the existing `secp256k1_u128` primitives to capture the remaining 11 cycles.
Fantastic. Happy to close #453 and hand the change over to this PR.

Pushed commit e282b48 integrating the branchless 258-to-256 tail from #453 into `secp256k1_scalar_reduce_512`, expressed using `secp256k1_uint128` primitives and shared across both the portable C and x86_64 assembly paths. This eliminates the duplicate assembly Phase 3 and the conditional branch in `secp256k1_scalar_reduce`, reducing total lines by 24 while maintaining a single 128-bit accumulator across the entire function.

Algebraic soundness holds unconditionally over all 512-bit inputs. Since `p4 <= 2` after Phase 2, the intermediate scalar `X = p0..p3 + p4 * SECP256K1_N_C` is strictly bounded by `2^256 + 2 * (2^128 + 2^32 + 977) < 2N`. Folding an extra `SECP256K1_N_C` via `++p4` yields `X' = X + SECP256K1_N_C = 2^256 + (X - N)`. For `N <= X < 2N`, `X'` overflows bit 256, leaving the low 256 bits already canonical in `[0, N)` with a carry of 1. Decrementing `p4` yields mask 0, turning the recovery accumulation into a no-op. For `0 <= X < N`, no overflow occurs, carry is 0, decrementing `p4` yields `UINT64_MAX`, and accumulating `N` restores canonical `X` with a final carry of 1 canceling `p4` (`acc + p4 == 0`).

SMT QF_BV formal verification confirms unsat across all four reduction invariant queries, while negative control mutants (omitted increment, inverted mask, 32-bit truncated mask) emit expected sat counterexamples. Disassembly of the generated binary confirms a purely straight-line sequence with zero conditional branches (`je`, `jne`, `jb`). Serialized `__rdtscp` benchmarks over 100,000 iterations clock `scalar_mul` at 182 cycles on portable C and 208 cycles on assembly on AMD Zen, capturing the latency gain without register spilling.

Tested ACK e282b48. Checked the test suite coverage actually exercises all cases, especially the problematic [N, 2^256) gap.

Some notes:

> In `secp256k1_scalar_reduce_512`, all limb multiplications involve either `SECP256K1_N_C_0` (`0x402da1732fc9bebf`, ~0.251 * 2^64) or `SECP256K1_N_C_1` (`0x551231950b75fc44`, ~0.332 * 2^64). Because both constants have bit 63 cleared and their sum is ~0.583 * 2^64, the accumulator across both reduction phases peaks at `0x953fd3083b3fbb04ffffffffffffffff` (~0.583 * 2^128) under worst-case 512-bit inputs. It never overflows 128 bits, so the carry into `c2` is always zero.

The value given here for SECP256K1_N_C_1 is wrong; I make it `~0xBAAEDCE6AF48A03BULL` i.e. **0x4551231950B75FC4**, and the accumulator bound is correspondingly lower, a little over 0.52 * 2^128.

> The algebraic soundness of the 258->256 trick holds unconditionally for all 512-bit inputs. With `p = p0..p3 + p4 * 2^256` and `p4 <= 3`, setting `X = p0..p3 + p4 * SECP256K1_N_C` guarantees `X < 2^256 + 3 * 2^129 < 2N`. Because `X < 2N`, `X` is strictly partitioned into `[0, N)` or `[N, 2N)`.

Particularly in the code comment ("X < 2N makes the carry a canonicality selector."), this definition for X is missing. I suggest a code comment along these lines instead (careful, X's definition changes):

    /* R = p[0..3] + p4*N_C is congruent to X = p[0..3] + p4*2^256 mod N,
     * and p4 <= 2 gives R < 2N. Dropping p4*2^256 and adding (p4+1)*N_C
     * computes R + N_C, whose carry out of limb 3 is 1 iff R >= N, leaving
     * R - N; otherwise adding N back leaves R. */

@Yudis-bit If you want to take the idea further (presumably in a separate PR), note that for such small remainder N_C, any value for p4 would work ("320 -> 256 tail") - except that the increment would wrap UINT64_MAX. It suggests the earlier phases could save some work, by only folding two limbs per step. Claude says that leaves a 65-bit p4..p5 value which still gives an efficient tail with the same shape.

events.message:
scalar: Use branchless 258-bit to 256-bit reduction in 4x64 reduce_512

Replace the 258-to-256-bit reduction and conditional overflow reduction
with the branchless sequence from PR 453.

By pre-incrementing p4, an extra SECP256K1_N_C is folded into the scalar.
Because X < 2N for any 258-bit intermediate in reduce_512, the resulting
carry out of limb 3 is strictly bounded to {0, 1} and acts as a
canonicality selector.

Decrementing p4 converts carry 0 into UINT64_MAX (adding N in the recovery
pass) and carry 1 into 0 (no correction needed).

The recovery pass and limb assignments are shared between the x86_64
assembly and portable C paths using secp256k1_uint128, eliminating inline
assembly Phase 3 and secp256k1_scalar_reduce entirely.

events.body:
Updated the code comment with your suggested phrasing and corrected the SECP256K1_N_C_1 constant and ~0.52 * 2^128 bound in the PR description.

The 320->256 tail is a neat direction. Because SECP256K1_N_C is under 2^129, R < 2N holds for any p4 < 2^126, so the carry selector logic generalizes directly to wider limbs without false carries.

Regarding the 2-limb folding schedule, folding l[6..7] produces l7 * 2^448 = l7 * (2^320 + N_C_1 * 2^256 + N_C_0 * 2^192). The top term spills carry m6 into bit 384 (limb 6). If Phase 2 only folds m4..m5, m6 remains unreduced at bit 384, and absorbing it in the tail re-injects N_C * 2^128 back into limbs 2 and 3.

Because m6 <= 1, folding m6 requires no 64x64 multiplications, only a conditional limb addition. Absorbing m6 additively at the end of Phase 1 leaves Phase 2 to fold strictly m4..m5, which saves four 64x64 multiplications and feeds a clean 320-bit input to the branchless tail. I will draft and verify this structure for the follow-up PR once this lands.

The cycle counts here are from AMD Zen, so I measured on arm64, against master and against #1951, which this PR builds on.

Apple M5, AppleClang 21, default `cmake` build (RelWithDebInfo, `-O2`), heads master 22245ae, #1951 a2d5d5b and #1954 ac77858, avg us:

| benchmark | master | #1951 | this PR | vs master | vs #1951 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| scalar_mul | 0.0219 | 0.0175 | 0.0158 | -28% | -10% |
| scalar_split | 0.0909 | 0.0754 | 0.0706 | -22% | -6% |
| scalar_inverse | 1.48 | 1.48 | 1.50 | +1.4% | +1.4% |
| scalar_inverse_var | 0.800 | 0.800 | 0.799 | 0% | 0% |
| ecmult_gen | 5.59 | 5.60 | 5.60 | +0.2% | 0% |
| ecmult_const | 12.0 | 11.9 | 11.9 | -0.8% | 0% |
| ecmult_1p_g | 5.76 | 5.80 | 5.79 | +0.5% | -0.2% |
| ecdsa_sign | 11.2 | 11.2 | 11.2 | 0% | 0% |
| ecdsa_verify | 14.6 | 14.6 | 14.6 | 0% | 0% |
| schnorrsig_verify | 14.8 | 14.8 | 14.8 | 0% | 0% |

Medians of 5 interleaved runs (`bench_internal scalar` at 1M iterations, `bench_ecmult`, `bench`) at 1-minute load under 3, one run at a time; spread at most 3.2% per row. 20 shorter runs of `bench_internal mul split inverse` agree within 1 point. `tests` passes.

On arm64 this PR makes `scalar_mul` another 10% faster than #1951. Constant-time `scalar_inverse` is 1.4% (about 20 ns) slower than master and #1951 (slower than master in all 25 runs, than #1951 in 23; the printed resolution is 10 ns); I have not looked into why. Whole operations stay within 1% of master.

Follow-up on the `scalar_inverse` row I posted (+1.4% for this PR vs #1951 on arm64): I checked where it comes from, and it is code placement, not slower code.

`scalar_inverse` does not call `scalar_mul` or `reduce_512`. In the `bench_internal` binaries, the functions it runs (`secp256k1_modinv64` and its helpers) are instruction-for-instruction identical in #1951 and this PR, apart from addresses. They sit 52 bytes earlier in this PR, because the code before them in the same translation unit is smaller. That moves the 132-byte inner loop (59 divsteps) from 56 to 4 mod 64. With `-falign-loops=64` the loop has the same alignment in both builds and the difference disappears: median `bench_internal inverse` over 30 interleaved runs is 1.50 µs for both, against 1.49 (#1951) and 1.51 (this PR) with default flags.

So the +1.4% is a layout effect of this build (AppleClang 21, `-O2`, Apple M5). Other compilers, flags or CPUs will place the code differently, so there it may be faster, slower or neutral.
